Chapter Two: The Chapter on the Root Mantra. Within this Samaya Sūtra, the root secret essentials of the Vidyārāja Acala are briefly expounded, which accomplish all activities.
In order to cause all practitioners to manifest the true wisdom of all Buddhas,
all Buddhas of the three periods of time, the Tathāgatas, Arhats,
and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, have done so by accomplishing the gateways of dhāraṇī and the gateways of samādhi.
Beneath the Bodhi tree, he manifested the realization of the three supreme doors of liberation and attained all-knowledge;
that Lion of the Śākyas did so because he had obtained the incomparable treasury of great vidyā-mantras.
It can subdue the armies of Māra and bring benefit and happiness to all;
therefore, the wise should settle their minds in this gateway and practice it in secret.
One should purify the bodhicitta and practice this dharma, for by doing so,
one will swiftly attain the accomplishment of all-knowledge. Thus says I,
the Bhagavān, the World-Honored One Mahāvairocana.
Furthermore, for the sake of removing obstacles for all those who practice mantras,
he dwelt in the fire-born samādhi and spoke this Great Mantra for Subduing Obstacles.
The majestic power of this secret vidyā can eliminate all manner of obstacles and difficulties for all sentient beings,
even unto the foot of the Bodhi tree.
By the power of this mantra,
all demonic armies will be utterly destroyed;
how much more so, then, all obstacles belonging to the world?
Furthermore, it is clarified that these obstacles are, in brief, of two kinds.
The first is internal obstacles,
which arise from one's own mind.
Their varieties are so numerous that they cannot be fully described.
Second are external obstacles,
which arise from the outside.
Their varieties are also very numerous;
to state the essentials,
they are all capable of removing hindrances.
He then spoke the wrathful mantra of the Noble Immovable Vidyārāja, the Great Destroyer of Obstacles:
*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇām | Trātāramogha-caṇḍa mahā-roṣaṇa sphoṭaya hūṃ trāsayatrāsaya hūṃ trāṭ haṃ kham*. The Secret Commentary explains:
Namo samanta-vajrāṇām. Homage to the Universal Wrathful Vajra Kings! Tāḍaya! Strike! Chinda! Sever! Bhinda! Destroy! Amogha-krodha! Unfailing Fury, the most extreme among the extremely fierce!
He manifests a form of extreme ferocity beyond compare;
he devours all obstacles in the world until none remain—this is the most evil among evils. *Mahāraudra* means "Great Wrath."
This is the most wrathful and violent among the extremely evil;
it is the primary meaning of all Buddhas.

*Vimarda* (vi-ma-da-ya) means to destroy and annihilate the nests of the world; *hūṃ* means to terrify; *tāḍaya* (tā-ra-ma-ya) means to make firm; *hūṃ tāḍa haṃ khaṃ* are the seed syllables. Use the final two characters (*haṃ khaṃ*) as the seed syllable.
Within all the meanings of these phrases, one is able to accomplish all activities.
The first, *caṇḍa*, signifies death;
yet by entering the gateway of the syllable *a*, it signifies that, fundamentally, there is neither birth nor death.
*Da* has the meaning of "struggle.
This refers to the Great King who is free from birth and death engaging in struggle with the four māras.
Next, *māra* has the meaning of "self."
Entering the gateway of the letter A is itself non-self;
it is also the samādhi of emptiness.
The letter Lu contains the letter Ra.
Its essence consists of the meaning of defilement-obstructions.
The presence of the sound *u* signifies samādhi;
that is, *śamatha* constitutes the great samādhi.
*Ña* has the meaning of "striving.
Entering the gateway of the syllable *A* is the Great Emptiness Samādhi (*mahāśūnyatā-samādhi*).
*Sa* has the meaning of "firmness."
This is likely the meaning of "foam":
because one knows that worldly phenomena are like a mass of foam, they are easily destroyed.
Beside it is the dot of the letter *a*, which signifies "action" (*saṃskāra*).
"Ṭa" has the meaning of "battle," signifying that which can oppose obstacles and fears so as to shatter them.
"Ya" has the meaning of "vehicle."
HŪṂ is the samādhi of great emptiness.
As explained above, TĀ is suchness (tathatā). RA is stainlessness.
*Ṭha* signifies "action," meaning that all phenomena are without action. The letter *Ha*,
with a dot above it (*visarga*), signifies the meaning of perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*).
It is also called the Wisdom of Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatājñāna*).
Entering the *ha*-gate signifies the meaning of practice (*caryā*).
Furthermore, there is the practice of the Vajra-samādhi of the syllable *a*, which terrifies māras and obstacles.
"Ya" is the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*).
By means of this practice of the immovable Great Emptiness, one greatly terrifies all demonic obstacles.
The syllable *MĀṂ* is also called the Wisdom of Great Emptiness.
The letter-gateway *ma* signifies the meaning of "self.
Entering the letter-gateway *a*, there is no self;
this means that all phenomena are fundamentally without arising or ceasing.
Furthermore, one uses this Great Emptiness and Selflessness Samādhi to terrify all Māras.
This syllable also contains the sounds *a* and *ya*. *A lu han mam*.
These four characters all contain the sound "A," which signifies the repeated terrifying of Māra and the ultimate state of dread;
it is the meaning of destroying both internal and external obstacles.
Having bound the samādhi,
one should immediately visualize one's own body as being entirely composed of the syllable *ḷa*.
This syllable should be visualized as having the color of fire.
From the syllable, a blazing, fierce flame issues forth,
incinerating the three poisons, the afflictions, and the secondary afflictions within the body;
when these are suddenly and completely exhausted at once, the fire also subsides accordingly.
Only the syllable *raṃ* remains, melting into a bright moon within the heart.
When performing this visualization, one should not linger;
quickly turn the mind of wisdom to bring it to accomplishment.

Chapter Three: Bathing and the Sealing and Protection of the Body. Section One: The Mudrā and Mantra of the Immovable Vajra for Utmost Peaceful Protection of the Body. First, interlace the two little fingers with their palms facing each other.
From the hollows between the thumbs, extend the two middle fingers and the two ring fingers straight upward,
with the two ring fingers crossed at the backs of the middle fingers.
Grasp the ring fingers with both index fingers, extend the two thumbs,
and press against the middle joints of the middle fingers; this is it.
The mantra is: Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Oṃ hola hola mahānimite hūṃ phaṭ. At that time, the Noble One Acala...
There are two kinds of methods for bathing:
first, internal purity;
second, external purity.
Internal purity means giving rise to the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings, being pure and free from the notion of self.
Second is external purity.
Whether bathing with water or in a river,
first bind the samaya-mudrā and place it upon the crown of the head;
recite the vidyā three times, and then use the vajra-mudrā and its vidyā to protect the body and wash away impurities.
Only then may one perform the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) with pure water and earth, also employing the mudrā and mantra of Acala-vajra.
Second: The Mudrā and Mantra for the Bathing and Protection of the Eight Directions by Acala-vajra. Form a fist by inserting the middle fingers into the palms.
Standing alone, advance to the Vajra Peak and perform three circumambulations:
turning to the right establishes the boundary;
turning to the left releases the boundary and performs the ritual of expulsion.

The mantra is: Oṃ haṃ hūṃ mahāhe maṃpadani paṃdha hūṃ paṃdha vajra vajre ṇi hūṃ phaṭ. This is the third *vidyā-mantra* for the bathing purification water of Acala-vajra. Regarding the *vidyā-mantra* for the bathing purification water of Acala-vajra: the wisdom and means enter into union; place them within the palms of the concentration and wisdom hands.
Stir the water with the seal to remove all obstacles.

The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantavajrāya trāṭ amogha-canda mahā-roṣaṇa sphoṭaya hūṃ trāsaya trāsaya hūṃ trāṭa hūṃ trāṭa*. This is the fourth mantra and mudrā for the Armor of Acala-vajra. Regarding the armor: place the palms together with the backs touching.
The force of advancement enters the palms in the same manner.
Join the six fingers together to form a three-pronged vajra;
then, opening the wrists, place the seal upon the body and crown, consecrating the five locations.
Scatter it upon the crown of the head;
this is called the Vajra Armor.
The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajrasamaye vajrakavace huṃ phaṭ. By sealing the five places with this mantra and mudrā, one becomes armored; then, according to one's wish, one may bathe.

5. The Mudrā and Mantra for the Empowerment of Acala-vajra. For the empowerment of Acala-vajra, the fifth: interlace the *tarjanī* (index) and *anāmikā* (ring) fingers inwardly; join the *madhyamā* (middle) and *kaniṣṭhā* (pinky) fingers upright;
and place the *tarjanī* (index) and *aṅguṣṭha* (thumbs) together.
The wisdom hand grasps the back of the other;
the same applies to the dhyāna hand.
This is called the mudrā of the consecration of the *iṣṭadevatā*.
The mantra is as follows:
*Namaḥ siddhārthāya, sarvatathāgatebhyo hṛdayasarvabuddhanilayaprapraśamanisāye abhiṣiñca tamo nudati jvalati vimalāye svāhā*. Thus is the mantra for the practitioner of truth.
Having donned armor to protect the body and finished bathing and dressing, one recites the vidyā:
Oṃ haṃ hūṃ saphaṭaya sahe hūṃ rakṣa haṃ phaṭ. This is the mantra of the seal of the immovable vajra-pestle.
Regarding the use of all impure places:
when a practitioner of true mantras wishes to go to any impure place, [they should proceed as follows].
First, seal the five locations with the mudrā of the pestle.
These are the two shoulders, the heart, the forehead, the throat, and the crown of the head.
When employing the mudrā:
Having empowered with the mantra, scatter [the flowers] above the crown of the head.
Recite the mantra:
Oṃ ajarakāñcana-candha svāhā hūṃ phaṭ. Chapter Four: Binding and Protecting the Maṇḍala. First: The Mantra and Seal of the Akṣobhya-vajra-samaya. Thus, having bathed according to the ritual rules:
He immediately went to the vihāra and,
with a pure mind, joined his palms as usual, holding the two fingers—
the wisdom finger (anāmikā) and the middle finger (madhyamā)— straight up.
Visualize the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas above the forehead as if they were standing directly before one's eyes,
and relax both body and mind.
With a mind of equanimity, one enters the samaya through the joy of dhyāna.
Reciting the vidyā, it says:
"The palms of the lotus hands, with dhyāna and prajñā joined together, empower the root vidyā and place it upon the forehead."
The power of aspiration stands upright and straight; wisdom forms the shape of a hook.
Prajñāpāramitā is pinched like a ring, and the wings of wisdom are likewise.
Then, with the swords of patience and diligence, one pierces them into the scabbard of meditative concentration.
This is called the Immovable Sword. To bind and protect the boundaries of the directions, draw the sword and circumambulate to the left;
to expel all māras, brandish the sword and rotate to the right, pointing it downward at the vajra-stake.
Above, bind the realm of space.
Then recite the secret mantra three or seven times in a low voice: *Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ trāṭ caṇḍa mahāraudra śatru phaṭ ya hūṃ trāṭ haṃ khaṃ*.
Binding the protection by turning the mudrā clockwise;
turning it counter-clockwise performs the expulsion, as well as the upward and downward movements.
This is the power of the vidyā.
It is capable of providing great protection for the great boundaries of the ten directions,
as well as protecting the body and purifying the location;
it can even provide defense throughout the three realms.
Moreover, when this Dharma is practiced in a particular place,
wherever the practitioner’s mental recitation of the vidyā-mantra and mudrā reaches, [it shall prevail].
It causes all various species and classes of difficult-to-tame malevolent spirits to behold the blazing wrath of the Vajra as a great mass of fire pervading that entire place.
The power of this mudrā is so vast that it is difficult to describe;
were one to remain in this world for an entire kalpa,
even then its power could not be fully exhausted.
This is called the Immovable Vajra Sword.
This mudrā and mantra are also applicable for the purposes of protecting the body and binding the boundary (sīmābandha) across the five families.
Extend the fingers of both hands apart, and join the thumbs and index fingers like a ring.
Each should erect a vajra-peak; this is called the Immovable Vajra.
Then recite the secret mantra: *Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ caṇḍa oṃ ajara-karṇa-caru-sādhye hūṃ phaṭ*. This vajra-mantra-seal can accomplish all activities.
Up to and including bathing, purifying the ground, protecting the body, and establishing the boundary, one employs this mantra and mudrā. To form the mudrā:

extend the fingers of the left hand and bend them into the palm; place the ring finger (kṣānti) and the little finger (praṇidhi) upright and side-by-side, with the thumb (dāna) and index finger (prajñā) joined together.
Fold the *dhyānāṅga* [fingers] and extend them downward; the *jñāna-aṅga* and *bala-aṅga* are likewise folded.
Recite the mantra:
Oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajramaṇḍale bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ (with a light *phaṭ*). Recite this mantra three times.
Rotate the mudrā three times counter-clockwise; according to the distance intended by the mind, the boundary wall is immediately accomplished.
Interlace the fingers of the hands of the *śīla-pāramitā* (the "Vow" hand) and *vīrya-pāramitā* (the "Diligence" hand) with the palms facing inward.

Extend the six fingers (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) vertically so that their tips touch, then open the wrists and rotate them three times clockwise above the crown of the head. This constitutes the adamantine, firm net.
Recite the mantra:
Oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajrasarvabuddhānī hūṃ phaṭ. Having bound this mudrā, recite the mantra three times.
Rotating clockwise three times above the crown,
the boundary of the net is established.
With both palms turned upward and backs crossed, the samādhi-fire of the principal deity is accomplished.
Three times circling outside the vajra wall, like a city of vajras with fierce flames, all the demonic armies are utterly dispersed.
Recite the mantra: OṂ HAṂ HŪṂ VAJRA-JVALA HŪṂ PHAṬ. Then, bind this flame mudrā.
Having recited the mantra three times,
one circumambulates three times to the right outside the vajra wall, whereby the fire enclosure is immediately formed.
The palms are placed level and steady, supporting the backs of the wisdom hands. The practitioner visualizes this as a vajra seat;
upon this seat, one further places the mudrā of one's chosen deity. All the noble ones rejoice in this, and the mantra is recited as follows:
Oṃ haṃ hūṃ vajrasādhane hūṃ phaṭ. By empowering the dwelling place with this mantra and mudrā, one attains the indestructible vajra ground.
One should then visualize a vajra-throne upon the ground. Thereupon,
one should place all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas upon the vajra-throne using the seal of the Tathāgata’s birth,
and then turn this seal to make offerings to the noble ones.
With the vajra-firm hands crossed within, the thumbs and wisdom fingers extended upward to form the mudrā born therefrom—this mudrā is named the Mother of Virtue.
Within it dwell the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;
by binding this secret seal, the vidyārājas and the tutelary deities all assemble like clouds.
Then, turning this mudrā to offer it to the various Honored Ones, one accomplishes the *argha* offering to the Buddhas:
*Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānām amogavikaradate 'riṣṭa svāhā*. One should then visualize this *tathāgatodbhava-mudrā* as the *argha*.
Offer this to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and venerable holy ones;
by constantly performing this Dharma-offering,
one will swiftly attain accomplishment.
Again, visualize the noble Acala residing in his original position.
Offer the previously mentioned consecration mudrā and mantra to the deity,
and then recite the root mantra once.
Because it can cause the noble ones to rejoice and swiftly bring about perfect accomplishment.
Furthermore, for the vidyādhara practitioner:

Next, bind the Samaya-mudrā and place it upon the crown of the head as previously described; then visualize oneself as the deity, seated upon an eight-petaled lotus flower and holding an incense burner in hand.
Immediately, one should cause the three karmas to become tranquil and free from distraction.
Proceeding to the vihāra, one arrives at the gate of the maṇḍala and utters the syllable HŪṂ three times to awaken all the noble ones.
Having entered the vihāra and placed [the image] upon it with the *samādhi-mudrā*,
one should next perform the ritual of prostration and confession as usual and offer *argha*.
One should then form this thought:
I now offer my entire body as an offering to the assembly at the sites of practice where the Three Jewels—eternally abiding throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time—are present.
I pray that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will [accept this].
We pray that you grant us great empowerment and supreme accomplishment,
so that we may attain the siddhi of Vajrasattva.
One should request protection for the sake of being gathered [into the mandala].
Having thus made the three requests, one proceeds as follows.

One should offer the seal produced by the Tathāgata to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,

Secretly recite the Soma-vajra mantra; confess all transgressions of the four periods.
With the power of the precepts advancing inward and the fingers mutually hooked, join the six pāramitās upward to form the Vajra-cakra seal.
Placing this mantra-seal upon the crown of the head, rotate it three times to the right to apologize for one's faults.
